lawyer:
Mr. Salauddin Abroad with Mr. Md. Ramzan Ali Sikder, Advocates ----- for the appellants. 
Mr. Ruhul Quddus ----- for the respondent No. 1.
parties:
Philip Morris Products Inc.
Vs.
National Tobacco Co. Ltd. and another
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This appeal is from decision dated 29.9.1999 passed by the Respondent No. 2, the Registrar of Trade Marks dismissing the application for the review of the order dated 9.12.1998 passed by the Respondent No. 2 rejecting the notice of opposition filed by the opponent-appellant being opposition case No. 1497 of 1998 arising out of Trade Mark Application No. 41692 in Class-34. 

 2. The respondent No. 1 filed Trade Mark Application No. 41692 for the registration of their mark "Gold Star" in class-34 and after the publication of the said mark in the Trade Mark Journal the appellant filed notice of opposition to that advertisement which was registered as opposition case No. 1497 of 1998 and the notice of opposition was rejected by the respondent No 2 vide his order dated 9.12.98 on the ground that the notice of opposition was filed beyond the time prescribed by law. Against this order of the Registrar the opponent-appellant filed an application for review on 23.3.99 and the review application too was rejected by the Registrar by the impugned order dated 29.9.99 on the ground that the appellant failed to file the opposition within the specified time and as such there is nothing to review the order rejecting the opposition and that order of rejection of the review petition is under challenge in this appeal. 

 3. Mr. Salahuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the opponent-appellant, submits that the review petition was filed against the decision and order of the respondent No. 2 dated 9.12.98 by the opponent-appellant in respect of the Trade Mark "Gold Star" advertised in the Trade Mark Journal No. 187 which was allegedly published in February, 1998 and that the notice of opposition was rejected by the Registrar on the sole ground that the said notice of opposition was filed 1 month 26 days after the expiry of 4 (four) months time limit as prescribed by Rule 30 of the revised Trade Marks Rule, 1963 and therefore the respondent No. 2 ought to have considered that fact that the said Trade Mark Journal as a matter of fact was circulated to the public on 26.5.1998 and therefore the respondent No. 2 ought to have allowed the review petition of the appellant on the ground that the notice of opposition in question was filed within the statutory period of 4 (four) months from the date of circulation of the Trade Mark Journal in question. The learned Advocate further submits that the impugned decision is a non-speaking one since the respondent No. 2 has not assigned any or any adequate reason for passing the same and therefore the same is liable to be set aside. The learned advocate further submits that the impugned decision is bad in law and not warranted by the facts and circumstances of the case and is laible to be set aside. 

 5. Mr. Salahuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the opponent-appellant, in reply submitted that if the contention raised by the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 is accepted that will lead to an absurd situation inasmuch as the statutory right of 4 months time limit to file the opposition from the date of publication of the advertisement will be curtailed and in some cases the aggrieved party will have no opportunity to file an opposition if the Journal is published after four months from the date of sending the same for publication. In elaborating his argument the learned Advocate submits that if an advertisement is published after 3 months from the date of communication made by the Registrar of Trade Marks with the office of the Forms and Publication then interested aggrieved party will have only one months time to file an opposition as against statutory period of four months and the statutory right to file an opposition within 4 months will be curtailed for no fault of the aggrieved person. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant case it cannot be said that the instant appeal has become infructuous inasmuch as the mark applied for by the applicant respondent No. 1 has been hurriedly registered before the expiry of the period of limitation for filing an appeal against the impugned order only to defeat the statutory right of the appellant, and in support of his contention is relied on the decision reported in PLD 1968 (Karachi) 363 wherein it has been held that the appealable order event if acted upon cannot escape consequences of appeal. 

 6. The admitted position is that the advertisement was published u/s. 15(1) of Trade Marks Act, 1940 (hereinafter called the Act") in the Journal No. 187 as shown in February, 1998 but from the materials on record it appears that the said Journal was sent by the respondent No. 2 for publication on 9.3.1998 and the said Journal was circulated to the public after receipt of copies of the same on 26.5.1998. Therefore it appears that in rejecting the notice of opposition the respondent No. 2 did not at all advert to this aspect of the case. He rejected the notice of opposition on the ground that it was filed long after 1 month and 26 days of the expiry of the statutory period of limitation of 4 months from February, 1998 but from the order sheet and the materials on record it appears that the aforesaid mark was sent for printing on 9.3.1998 and it was received back by the office of the respondent No. 2 on 26.5.1998 before which date no of member of the public had any access to the advertisement in question. Mr. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed a stressed much emphasis on the fact that the opposition must be filed within the prescribed time of four months from the date of the advertisement of the mark as contemplated in sub-section (2) of section 15 of the Act. Mr. Ahmed relying on the provisions of sub-section (2) of the section 15 of the Act read with Rule 30 of the revised Trade Marks Rules 1963 (hereinafter called 'the Rule') submitted that a plain reading of these provisions clearly indicate that the date mentioned in section 15 means the date appended in the Journal itself and not the actual date publication of the advertisement and therefore the Respondent No. 2 rightly rejecting the application by computing the statutory period of four months from the date appended in the Journal itself. In the course of argument we wanted to know from Mr. Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 what would be the position if an advertisement is published well after four months from the date appended in the Journal. Mr. Ahmed simply replied that that is not the case here but he could not give any reply what would happen in that case. If the contention of Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed is accepted that would lead to an absurd situation and the purpose of the legislation will be defeated and the aggrieved persons will be left with no remedy for no fault of them. Let us visualise a case where the mark is actually published well after four months from the date of sending it for publication. In that case if the date appended in the Journal is taken for computing the period of limitation then none of the aggrieved persons would be able to file notice of opposition even though it was actually published long after. Besides, if the advertisement is actually published after two months from the date of receipt of the same by the office then also the statutory period of four months will be reduced to two months. In each case the aggrieved person's statutory right will be denied. We have carefully examined the provision of sub-section (2) of section 15 and the same read with the provisions of Rule 30 it appears to us that date of advertisement means the date on which the advertisement was actually published in the Trade Marks Journal and the date on which it was circulated amongst the numbers of the public for subscription. In that view of the matter there is no hesitation in our mind in holding that in the instant case the respondent No. 2 under misconception of law and misinterpreting the provisions of section 15(2) and Rule 30 rejected the notice of opposition illegally on the sole ground of limitation. Be that as it may, against that order the appellant filed a review application and that review application was rejected by the respondent No. 2 by the impugned order simply on the ground that since the appellant had failed to file the opposition within the statutory period of limitation, there was no scope of considering the review application. It is therefore clear that the respondent No. 2, Registrar of Trade Mark, without entering into the merits of the review application has rejected the same mechanically on the ground that as the petitioner failed to file the notice of opposition within the statutory period of 4 months there was no scope to entertain the review application thereon. But from our discussions in the foregoing paragraphs, it is clear that in the instant case the notice of opposition was filed well within the statutory period of limitation and in rejecting the review petition the respondent No. 2 did not take into the consideration that aspect of the case although the issue was raised before the Registrar by the appellant. It is not the case of the respondents that no review lies but the review application has been rejected on the ground that since the appellant failed to file the opposition within the period of limitation, there is no scope to entertain it. This cannot be a valid ground for rejecting the review application without entering into the merits of the application, more so when the opposition was filed within time. 

 7. From the materials on record it appears that the impugned decision suffers from patent illegality and the impugned order cannot be maintained on the ground that the mark has already been registered. In the instant case the Registrar registered the mark before the expiry of period of limitation for filing an appeal against the impugned order and that shows the mala fide on the part of the Registrar. In all fairness he ought to have waited till the time for filing appeal expires. The granting of registration of the mark of the respondent No. 1 cannot be a ground for treating the instant appeal infructuous. In the case of the Province of West Pakistan Versus. Muhammad Jaman reported in PLD, 1960 (Karachi) 908, it has been held; 

 Following this decision the case of Aktiebola Get Jonkoping Vulcan -Vs- The Registrar of Trade Marks and another reported in PLD, 1968 Karachi, 363, it has been held that an appealable order cannot escape the consequences of appeal merely because it has been acted upon. Thus if the appellant succeeds the registration will automatically go and the proceedings will be revived at that stage where the impugned order was passed. So, we do not find any substance in the submissions of Mr. Khandakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed. 

 8. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The impugned decision is set aside and the case is sent back to the respondent No. 2 for disposing of the review application in accordance with law.
